Due to this inherent instability, modeling, monitoring, and ensuring the permanent storage of injected CO₂ present significant challenges. Only a limited number of locations are likely to qualify for long-term CO sequestration if they adhere to 2 rigorous hydrological and geological assessments. It may take over a decade to obtain the necessary geological details of Florida's geology. Consequently, stakeholders are actively considering marine transportation for exporting captured CO , as it presents an attractive option in terms of efficiency, risk 2 reduction, cost, and time to commercial operation. Marine transport is likely to be the only viable alternative for many emitters, particularly for those located near the coast. It is these unusual geological features of Florida that are currently thought to make it generally unsuitable for safe, permanent sequestration of CO which makes the export of captured CO out of Florida on a 2 2 marine transportation system even more critical as the best solution for Florida emitters. 3.1.2 THE PROPOSED T-RICH SITE In 2005 soil borings were taken on a site adjacent to the proposed T-RICH site, approximately 2,000 feet east of where the T-RICH CO storage tanks are proposed to be placed on the Pendola Point peninsula. 2 Those borings found various layers of silty clayey sand, sandy clay to clay, and slightly silty to silty sand generally down to a depth of 45 to 50 feet. Below 50 feet lies a layer of weathered to completely weathered limestone, and at a depth below approximately 70 feet slightly weathered limestone is encountered. Groundwater was found at a depth of 8 to 10 feet with a note that the seasonal high level of groundwater should be expected to be 6 to 8 feet below the surface.5 The borings were taken in preparation for the construction of cement storage domes with a noted design weight of 45,000 tons. The weight of CO tanks taking up an equivalent amount of ground surface area is only approximately 6,500 2 tons. The report recommended the use of precast concrete piles or drilled shaft foundations with a 5 to 10 foot penetration into the limestone layer, for a total pile depth of approximately 60 feet.
